questions.question: How do you annotate collections and generic types in Python?
questions.title: Collection and Generic Type Hints in Python
questions.direct_answer: Put the contained types in square brackets: `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, `set[int]`, or `tuple[str, ...]`. For an interface, prefer an abstract type such as `Sequence[str]` or `Iterable[str]`; use a type variable when an input type must be connected to an output type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can express both a container and the types carried inside it, and whether you understand a reusable type variable.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing only `list` or `dict`, which usually leaves their contained values as `Any` to a checker.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish a concrete mutable collection from an input capability such as `Iterable` or `Sequence`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `list[str]`, `set[int]`, and `dict[str, float]` to describe contained values.
Use `tuple[int, str]` for fixed positions and `tuple[int, ...]` for any number of integers.
Use `Iterable[T]` for one-pass iteration and `Sequence[T]` when indexing and length are required.
A type variable connects the same unknown type across inputs and outputs.
Built-in generics such as `list[str]` require Python 3.9 or newer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A collection annotation describes two things: the kind of container and the type of values inside it. `list[str]` means a mutable list of strings, while `dict[str, int]` means string keys mapped to integer values.

Tuple syntax depends on shape. `tuple[str, int]` describes exactly two positions with different types, and `tuple[int, ...]` describes any-length tuple whose items are all integers.

For parameters, I type the capability the function actually needs. For example, a function that only loops can accept `Iterable[str]`; one that also uses `len()` and indexing can accept `Sequence[str]`; one that appends in place genuinely needs a mutable collection such as `list[str]`.

Generics preserve a relationship rather than naming one fixed type. With a type variable `T`, a function from `Sequence[T]` to `T` says that the result has the same element type as its input.

The modern built-in spelling works from Python 3.9. Code supporting Python 3.8 may still use `typing.List`, `typing.Dict`, and related aliases. These hints guide checkers; they do not inspect every element at runtime.

sections.title: Describe both shape and relationship
sections.content:
A bare container type loses the information that matters after an item is read. If a checker knows only `list[Any]`, operations on each item can silently escape checking. Once it knows `list[User]`, it can verify appends, indexing, iteration, and method calls on the resulting `User`.

Abstract collection types make an API less demanding. `Iterable[T]` promises only that values can be produced one at a time. `Sequence[T]` adds stable order, length, and integer indexing. A concrete `list[T]` adds list-specific mutation. Choosing the smallest required promise gives callers more valid choices.

A type variable represents one type chosen consistently for a particular call. It is different from `Any`: `Any` disables important checks, while `T` lets the checker discover a concrete type and carry it through the operation.

sections.title: Collection hints carry progressively stronger promises
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I[Iterable T: can loop] --> S[Sequence T: loop, len, index]
  S --> L[list T: sequence plus mutation]
  G[Generic T] --> I
  G --> S
  G --> L
  L --> E[Reading an item produces T]
```

sections.title: Keep the element type from input to output
sections.content:
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")

def first(items: Sequence[T]) -> T:
    if not items:
        raise ValueError("items must not be empty")
    return items[0]

scores: list[int] = [8, 13, 21]
labels: dict[str, int] = {"open": 2, "closed": 5}
print(first(scores) + 1)
print(labels["open"])
```

For this call, the checker binds `T` to `int`, so the result of `first(scores)` is also known to be `int`.

questions.question: When should a Python parameter use Iterable, Sequence, or list?
questions.title: Iterable vs Sequence vs list in Type Hints
questions.direct_answer: Use `Iterable[T]` when the function only consumes items in a loop, `Sequence[T]` when it also needs length or indexing, and `list[T]` when it depends on list-specific mutation or methods. The parameter should promise only the operations the implementation requires.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you design a parameter around required behaviour rather than the one concrete type used by the first caller.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Typing every collection parameter as `list`, which rejects valid tuples, ranges, or generators without a real need.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out that an iterable may be single-pass, so code that loops twice needs a stronger contract or a local copy.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Iterable[T]` guarantees that the function can obtain items one by one.
`Sequence[T]` also provides length, stable order, and integer indexing.
`list[T]` is appropriate when the function uses list-specific mutation.
A generator is iterable but not a sequence and may be exhausted after one pass.
Accept a broad interface and return a concrete type when that matches the work.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I choose among `Iterable`, `Sequence`, and `list` by looking at which operations the function performs. `Iterable[T]` is enough when the body makes one pass with a `for` loop and does not require a length or an index.

`Sequence[T]` is a stronger read-only-style input contract. It supports `len(items)`, integer indexing, and repeated traversal, so lists and tuples both fit. For example, a function that compares the first and last names can ask for `Sequence[str]` without requiring callers to build a list.

I use `list[T]` when list behaviour is part of the contract, such as appending, sorting in place, or replacing an indexed item. If the function does not mutate, requiring a list is needlessly narrow.

One boundary matters with `Iterable`: a generator may be consumed after one pass and has no guaranteed length. If the algorithm needs several passes, I require a sequence or materialize the iterable once with `list(items)`.

This choice affects API flexibility, not normal runtime validation. The element annotation is still checked by tooling rather than enforced as values arrive.

sections.title: Model the operations, not today's caller
sections.content:
An input type is a promise the caller must satisfy. Every extra method in that promise removes possible callers. A loop needs less than an index lookup, and an index lookup needs less than in-place mutation. Starting from actual operations therefore produces an honest and reusable interface.

`Iterable` includes lists, tuples, sets, generators, files, and many custom objects. That breadth comes with a limit: the protocol promises an iterator, not replay, order, indexing, or length. `Sequence` narrows the family to ordered, indexable, sized values. `list` then commits the function to one mutable concrete implementation.

A function can accept a broad input and still return a predictable concrete output. For example, a normalization function may consume any iterable once and return a new `list[str]`; callers get flexibility without ambiguity about the result.

sections.title: Choose from the operations used
sections.content:
| Annotation | Guaranteed operations | Example accepted values | Main caution |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Iterable[T]` | Produce items for iteration | list, tuple, set, generator | May be single-pass; no `len()` or index promise |
| `Sequence[T]` | Iterate, `len()`, integer index | list, tuple, range, str | Does not promise list mutation |
| `list[T]` | Sequence operations plus list mutation | list | Needlessly excludes tuples and generators when mutation is not used |

sections.title: Accept broadly and return clearly
sections.content:
```python
from collections.abc import Iterable, Sequence

def cleaned(items: Iterable[str]) -> list[str]:
    return [item.strip() for item in items if item.strip()]

def endpoints(items: Sequence[str]) -> tuple[str, str]:
    if not items:
        raise ValueError("items must not be empty")
    return items[0], items[-1]

print(cleaned(name for name in [" Ada ", "", " Lin "]))
print(endpoints(("first", "middle", "last")))
```

The first function needs only one pass, while the second honestly asks for indexing and length.

questions.question: Why should list and dict annotations include their contained types?
questions.title: Avoid Bare Collection Type Hints
questions.direct_answer: A bare `list` or `dict` does not tell a checker what comes out of the collection; checkers commonly treat missing type arguments as `Any`. Writing `list[User]` or `dict[str, int]` lets the checker verify inserts, lookups, iteration, and later operations on each value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that a generic container needs type arguments to preserve useful information.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using bare collections or `Any` everywhere and believing the file is now meaningfully typed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how an `Any` value propagates and can hide invalid method calls or assignments.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Bare `list` usually loses the element type as `Any`.
Bare `dict` loses both key and value types.
Parameterized collections let a checker verify both writes and reads.
`Any` permits almost every operation and can spread through later expressions.
Use `object` for an unknown value that must be narrowed safely.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A collection type without arguments says too little. If a parameter is only `list`, a checker commonly treats its elements as `Any`, so reading `items[0]` gives a value on which almost any method call is allowed.

Parameterizing the collection preserves the next piece of the data model. `list[str]` lets the checker reject an integer append and know that iteration produces strings; `dict[str, int]` verifies keys, assigned values, and the type returned by a lookup.

For example, a bare list can let `item.nonexistent()` pass static analysis because `item` is `Any`. With `list[str]`, the checker knows that a string has no such method and reports the error before execution.

`Any` is different from `object`. Both can represent an unknown runtime value, but `object` forces code to narrow with `isinstance` before using type-specific operations, while `Any` effectively turns those checks off.

I therefore fill in collection type arguments whenever the element shape is known, and enable a checker option such as mypy's `disallow_any_generics` when a project wants to prevent accidental bare generics.

sections.title: Container element types and the values they produce
sections.content:
A useful way to read a generic is from right to left: `dict[str, list[int]]` says that indexing by a string produces a list, and indexing that list produces an integer. Each type argument carries information to the next operation. Omitting an argument breaks that chain.

`Any` is deliberately permissive for gradual migration and hard-to-type integration points. A checker accepts assignments to and from it and usually treats results of its operations as more `Any`. That makes it convenient, but a small unintentional leak can hide errors far from where the unknown value entered.

When the element truly is unknown, prefer `object` until runtime checks establish more information. Use `Any` consciously at a narrow boundary, not as the default spelling for a collection whose element type is already known.

sections.title: Type information follows each lookup
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D[dict str, list int] -->|lookup by str| L[list int]
  L -->|index or iterate| I[int]
  B[bare dict] -->|lookup| A[Any]
  A -->|almost any operation accepted| A2[more Any]
```
